criteria.description: Identifies that 'steepest' is only meaningful relative to a chosen notion of distance/metric.
Explains that the plain gradient is steepest specifically under the Euclidean metric, and gives a concrete reason a different metric (e.g. mismatched units/scales) breaks that.

commonErrors: Saying the gradient is 'just wrong' in general, without identifying that it's correct under one specific (Euclidean) assumption.
Not connecting the units/scale example back to the abstract metric concept.

solutions.fullSolution: 'Steepest descent' means: among all directions of a fixed 'length', which one decreases f the most. That notion of length requires choosing a metric. The plain gradient direction is steepest specifically under the standard Euclidean metric, where a unit step means d^T d = 1, i.e. every coordinate direction is treated as costing the same amount of movement. If coordinates have different physical scales or units (millimeters vs meters, or more generally after a nonlinear change of variables), a Euclidean unit step in one coordinate corresponds to a very different amount of actual physical movement than a Euclidean unit step in another coordinate. So the direction that looks steepest when measured in raw, unit-blind coordinates isn't actually the direction that decreases f the most per unit of real, physically meaningful movement.

criteria.description: Correctly sets up the Lagrangian for the constrained minimization.
Correctly differentiates and sets partial L/partial d = 0, getting grad f(x) + 2*lambda*G*d = 0.
Correctly solves for d and identifies that the scalar factor only affects length, not direction, giving d* proportional to -G^-1 grad f(x).

commonErrors: Forgetting the factor of 2 from differentiating the quadratic constraint d^T G d.
Not explaining why the scalar 1/(2*lambda) doesn't matter for the DIRECTION of steepest descent, only its magnitude.

solutions.fullSolution:
Lagrangian: L(d,lambda) = grad_f(x)^T d + lambda(d^T G d - 1). Setting partial L/partial d = 0: grad_f(x) + 2*lambda*G*d = 0, so G*d = -(1/(2*lambda)) grad_f(x), hence d = -(1/(2*lambda)) G^-1 grad_f(x).

The scalar 1/(2*lambda) is positive (chosen to satisfy the unit-length constraint d^T G d=1) and only rescales d's magnitude, not its direction. So the steepest-descent DIRECTION is d* proportional to -G^-1 grad_f(x). This is exactly the covariant gradient: -G^-1 grad_f(x) rather than the plain -grad_f(x), correcting for the geometry encoded by G.
G^-1 = [[0.5,0],[0,2]] (reciprocals of diagonal entries, since G is diagonal). G^-1 @ grad = [0.5*6, 2*13] = [3, 26]. d = -G^-1 @ grad = [-3,-26]. Second component: -26.
